---
title: "Medication"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-02-01"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

Pharmacotherapy remains an indispensable component even when other biological treatments are employed. Although medication is also known to exert its effects by enhancing neuroplasticity, its characteristics differ somewhat from other plasticity-enhancing treatments. Medication provides consistent stimuli that facilitate neural reorganization by maintaining stable neurotransmitter levels. This mechanism allows for a high degree of precision, as the gentle and gradual rewiring process supports the modification of synapses specifically "tagged" for reorganization. However, this subtle nature is often insufficient to disrupt the deeply ingrained pathological circuits in treatment-resistant patients. To understand how pharmacotherapy can complement or support other therapeutic interventions, it is useful to examine its effects through the lens of the DPRH framework.

## Disruption

Acute SSRI administration produces an immediate surge in synaptic serotonin concentration followed by a compensatory decrease in serotonergic tone during the first one to two weeks of treatment. This neurochemical destabilization may constitute a disruption phase. Only after chronic administration does enhanced serotonergic transmission become established in cortical and limbic projection regions.

The initial serotonergic perturbation translates into measurable network-level alteration. Even a single dose of escitalopram in healthy volunteers decreased functional connectivity within the DMN [@vandeVen2013] and produced widespread FC changes across multiple resting-state networks [@Klaassens2015]. These findings indicate that acute serotonergic modulation can rapidly perturb the organization of large-scale brain networks. In patients with major depressive disorder, Dutta et al.[@Dutta2019] demonstrated that acute intravenous citalopram rapidly reconfigured DMN intra-network connectivity, modifying the aberrant inclusion of the amygdala within the DMN that characterizes the depressed state.

These rapid neural changes precede any alteration in subjective mood and may be related to the initial side effects of SSRI treatment. The increased anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and irritability during the first days of treatment affects between 4% and 65% of patients initiating antidepressant therapy [@Sinclair2009]. Similarly, the rapid blockade of rewarding and aversive stimulus processing may explain the emotional blunting reported by a substantial proportion of SSRI-treated patients [@McCabe2010]. Much as the disruption induced by ECT produces temporary cognitive impairments, the perturbation in the early phase of pharmacotherapy may represent a necessary transitional stage for subsequent therapeutic benefit, though it offers little immediate gain for the patient.

## Potentiation

From this stage onward, pharmacotherapy begins to exert pronounced neuroplastic effects. As early as 1995, it was demonstrated that chronic antidepressant administration significantly increased BDNF and TrkB mRNA expression in the rat hippocampus [@Nibuya1995]. This finding gave rise to the neurotrophic model of depression [@Duman1997; @Duman2006]. More recent meta-analyses have confirmed that SSRI treatment increases peripheral BDNF levels in depressed patients [@Zhou2017].

Early neuroplasticity theories emphasized hippocampal neurogenesis as a primary mechanism. Malberg et al. [@Malberg2000] demonstrated that chronic antidepressant treatment significantly increased the birth of new neurons in the dentate gyrus. Further evidence showed that the ablation of neurogenesis via irradiation abolished the behavioral effects of both fluoxetine and imipramine in mice [@Santarelli2003]. However, the reliance on neurogenesis as the central mechanism was challenged by Bessa et al.[@bessa2008], who demonstrated that antidepressant effects persisted even when neurogenesis was blocked using methylazoxymethanol (MAM). Consequently, attention has shifted toward dendritic remodeling and changes in spine density within key brain regions as the critical mediators of therapeutic effects.

While the effect of SSRIs on serotonergic tone is more modest than that of psychedelics, it similarly reopens critical periods of heightened plasticity [@Vetencourt2008]. This phenomenon reflects serotonin's role as a gating mechanism for neuroplasticity [@Singer1995; @Kirkwood2000]. However, both psychedelics and SSRIs can directly bind to the transmembrane domain of TrkB neurotrophin receptors, promoting BDNF signaling through a mechanism independent of increased serotonergic tone [@Casarotto2021; @Moliner2023].

## Rewiring

SSRIs promote dendritic remodeling and spine density changes. Even short-term fluoxetine treatment (five days) induced a robust increase in pyramidal cell dendritic spine synapse density in the hippocampus [@Hajszan2005], and the degree of dendritic reorganization correlates with mood-elevating effects [@Bessa2009].

These synaptic-level changes translate into local and global connectivity alterations. Longitudinal neuroimaging studies consistently demonstrate that SSRI treatment normalizes the hyperconnectivity within the DMN [@Posner2013]. A large-scale neuroimaging analysis (more than 1,000 depressed patients) confirmed that medicated patients showed reduced DMN functional connectivity relative to unmedicated patients [@Yan2019]. These changes do not represent random rewiring; rather, they reflect the normalization of anomalous resting-state functional network configurations characteristic of the depressed state [@Dichter2015].

The strengthening of prefrontal regulatory control over limbic structures represents perhaps the most significant change during SSRI treatment. Anand et al. [@Anand2005] demonstrated that six weeks of sertraline treatment significantly increased functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex and limbic regions, reversing the corticolimbic disconnection observed in the depressed state. A subsequent study revealed that as corticolimbic connectivity increased with treatment, limbic activation to negative stimuli decreased [@Anand2007]. These findings suggest that medication did not simply attenuate limbic hyperactivation but fundamentally restructured the regulatory relationship between cortical and subcortical centers.

This rewiring process appears to consolidate the cognitive changes observed early in treatment into therapeutically meaningful outcomes. Catherine Harmer and colleagues proposed a cognitive neuropsychological model that accounts for the delayed onset of therapeutic effect [@Harmer2009]. Their work showed that SSRIs produced rapid changes in emotional information processing within hours to days of initiating treatment [@Harmer2009; @Godlewska2021], and the degree of this change could predict long-term antidepressant response [@Dichter2015]. According to this model, the therapeutic delay reflects the time required for corrected emotional processing biases to translate into sustained mood improvement through ongoing social and environmental interactions [@Harmer2017]. Within the DPRH framework, the early shift in emotional processing bias, coupled with enhanced plasticity, constitutes the necessary precondition for the emergence of more adaptive circuit configurations.
